modeNote: Explanatory walkthrough: the order, routes and outcomes follow the RTL, but the timing is not cycle-accurate and no simulation trace is replayed.

local.name: Local
local.carries: signals inside one tile, not on the network

scenarios.name: Boot and measure
scenarios.where: Board design; behaviour checked in simulation
scenarios.summary: Both processors start the demo firmware. Tile 3's instruction memory is sampled so that it can be measured.

events.label: Measurement window
events.what: The first 64 bytes of tile 3's instruction memory go to the PQ-Attest endpoint.
events.why: They are hashed with SHA3-256, together with the tile ID and configuration, to form the tile's measurement.
events.plain: Tile 3’s firmware is read so that it can be measured.
events.matters: The measurement is a fingerprint of the code: changed firmware gives a different fingerprint.

scenarios.name: Attest tile 3
scenarios.where: Board design; behaviour checked in simulation
scenarios.summary: The root of trust on tile 4 challenges tile 3, checks the answer and grants access. Tiles 4 and 3 are one hop apart.

events.label: CHALLENGE
events.what: The verifier sends a fresh 224-bit challenge to tile 3.
events.why: A fresh value stops an old answer from being replayed. The packet is authenticated by the L2 link.
events.plain: The root of trust challenges tile 3 to prove it can be trusted.
events.matters: A fresh challenge each time means an old answer cannot be replayed.

events.label: RESPONSE
events.what: Tile 3 returns its measurement and a KMAC128 tag (512-bit payload).
events.why: Only a tile holding the right key and running the expected firmware can produce a tag the verifier accepts.
events.plain: Tile 3 answers with its firmware fingerprint, sealed with a secret key.
events.matters: Only genuine hardware running the expected firmware can give a correct answer.

events.label: GRANT
events.what: The verifier accepts the answer and sends GRANT.
events.why: From now on tile 3 is authorized to use the shared memory.
events.plain: The answer is correct, so the root of trust grants tile 3 access.
events.matters: Until now tile 3 could not use the shared memory at all.

scenarios.name: Authorized memory access
scenarios.where: Board design; behaviour and latency measured in simulation
scenarios.summary: Tile 3 writes a value to the shared memory on tile 2 and reads it back over the network.

events.label: Write request
events.what: CPU A writes 0xC0DE5A5A. The request travels 3 to 4 to 5 to 2.
events.why: XY routing goes along X first, then Y. The memory front end checks that tile 3 is authorized before the write happens.
events.plain: Tile 3 writes the value 0xC0DE5A5A into the shared memory on tile 2.
events.matters: The memory checks the sender’s permission at the moment of the write.

events.label: Write response
events.what: The acknowledgement returns 2 to 1 to 0 to 3.
events.why: Responses use their own virtual channel, so they cannot be blocked behind requests.
events.matters: Replies travel on their own channel, so they never queue behind requests.

events.label: Read request
events.what: CPU A asks for the same address.
events.why: Authorization is checked again for this access.
events.plain: Tile 3 asks to read the same address.
events.matters: Permission is checked again on every access, not just once.

events.label: Read response
events.what: The stored value comes back and matches.
events.why: The firmware reports success on the UART and the LEDs.
events.plain: The value comes back and matches. Tile 3 prints “T3 PASS”.
events.matters: The trusted path works end to end.

scenarios.name: Refused tile
scenarios.where: Board design; behaviour checked in simulation
scenarios.summary: Tile 0 tries the same write. It was never authorized.

events.label: Local refusal
events.what: CPU B's request stops at its own bridge.
events.why: The bridge never raises a network request while the tile is not authorized, so no packet enters the mesh. The processor gets a poison value.
events.plain: Tile 0 tries the same write and is stopped inside its own tile.
events.matters: An untrusted tile never gets a single packet onto the network.

scenarios.name: Revoke
scenarios.where: Board design; behaviour checked in simulation
scenarios.summary: Button 2 makes the root of trust revoke tile 3. Button 1 would attest it again.

events.label: REVOKE
events.what: The verifier sends REVOKE to tile 3.
events.why: Tile 3 loses its authorization at once.
events.plain: Button 2 is pressed and the root of trust revokes tile 3’s access.
events.matters: Trust can be taken away while the chip runs, not only at power-on.

events.label: Refused request
events.what: CPU A's next memory request stops at its own bridge.
events.why: With authorization gone, the bridge refuses locally, exactly as tile 0's does.
events.plain: Tile 3’s next request is now stopped inside its own tile.
events.matters: Once revoked, tile 3 is treated like any untrusted tile.

scenarios.name: Forged packet
scenarios.where: Simulation only: the SPOOF port is tied off in the board image
scenarios.summary: An attack test: the untrusted port injects a forged or replayed packet.

events.label: Rejected at quarantine
events.what: The forged packet reaches the ingress quarantine and is rejected.
events.why: Packets from the untrusted port are held and checked first; forged control packets also fail the L2 tag and sequence check.
events.plain: A forged packet is injected and rejected by the quarantine. This runs in simulation only.
events.matters: Fake security messages cannot get into the network.
